sentences.text: You've seen it happen: a few lines of PySpark come back instantly, and then one line takes minutes.
Here are four lines, run on our cast scaled up to about a million rows.
The first three read nothing. Not one row.
The fourth reads every single row. So why do the first three read nothing?
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: nothing happens until you ask.
Back to our 103 patients. Line one filters them down to the higher-risk patients. Or rather, it writes that down.
A step is added to a plan: filter. Not one row moves.
Line two adds a column, and line three keeps just two columns. Each one adds a step.
Three lines, and not a single row has been read.
A DataFrame isn't a table of rows. It's a recipe: where the rows come from, and the steps to follow.
Line four asks a question: how many rows are left? That's an action, and an action runs the recipe.
The driver sends 4 tasks down, one per file.
Each task reads its file and filters the rows as they arrive, in a single pass.
And the new column? A count doesn't need it, so Spark never computes it. It even reads just the one column the filter needs.
46 higher-risk patients make it through, and one number goes up to the driver: 46.
Line five asks to see the rows. Another action, so the recipe runs again, from the files.
This time it needs every step, and it still makes one pass: filter, add the column, keep two.
Spark didn't keep the count's work. Normally, every action starts again from storage, unless you ask Spark to keep a result.
And even that request waits for an action. That's episode 10.
So why be lazy? Because when the action arrives, Spark sees the whole recipe at once, and can plan it.
Here's our cast again, written with its files sorted by risk.
Spark pushes the filter into the read itself. Files that hold no higher-risk patients are skipped, and it reads 53 rows instead of 103.
Episode 6 shows how.
So, two kinds of line. A transformation hands back a new DataFrame: a longer recipe, and no work.
An action hands back a result: a number, rows on screen or in your hands, or files written. Actions do the work.
A common exception: read a CSV file and ask Spark to guess its column types, and it runs 2 jobs, to look at the data.
Give it the schema, and the read is lazy again.
Let's gather it up.
Transformations write the recipe. Actions run it, in one pass over each pile.
And normally, every action starts again from storage.
One loose end: our count was one action, yet Spark ran it as 2 jobs and 2 stages.
How does Spark cut up the work? Next time: cut at the walls.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
